entries.title: OlmoEarth v1.3: State-of-the-art embeddings for the whole planet
entries.content:
allenai/OlmoEarth-v1_3-Base

Image Feature Extraction • Updated • 91 • 4

OlmoEarth v1.3: State-of-the-art embeddings for the whole planet

Enterprise Article

🤗 Models | 📄 Tech Report | 📊 Data | 💻 Code | 🌎 Embeddings Explorer | 🗺️ Interactive story

Today, we’re releasing OlmoEarth v1.3, a state-of-the-art satellite embedding model. Alongside OlmoEarth v1.3, we’re sharing precomputed, annual embeddings for the whole planet (10m, 64- and 128-dimensions), plus a new browser-based tool to explore and customize maps based on those embeddings — the OlmoEarth Embeddings Explorer. This means anyone can put OlmoEarth v1.3 to work right away, from tracking change over time to finding similar places—no sign-in, and no advanced technical knowledge required.

Until now, the primary way to use OlmoEarth was fine-tuning in OlmoEarth Studio: training a model for each task and running it over satellite imagery to make a map. That requires GPU access and the ability to download and store the imagery. Embedding models compress satellite data into ready-to-use features that can be reused cheaply for many tasks.

With OlmoEarth v1.3, we’re excited to give users more ways to explore and engage with planetary artifacts in whatever way suits them best.

Compute once, reuse everywhere

An embedding represents what the model learned from millions of images. OlmoEarth v1.3 reads a year of radar (Sentinel-1) and multispectral (Sentinel-2 and Landsat) satellite time series and produces one 128-dimensional vector for every 10-meter pixel on Earth; the first 64 dimensions also work on their own as a smaller embedding.

Foundation models and global embeddings are expensive to produce, and to make sure everyone is able to access the benefits, we’ve computed these embeddings for the entire planet and shared them with the community on Source Cooperative. From there, a crop map, a land-cover map, or a change analysis becomes a lightweight modeling problem: train a small classifier on top and run it locally.

How OlmoEarth v1.3 makes an embedding: a vision transformer reads the satellite data, an Attention Pooler pools it into one vector per patch of land, and a linear layer reduces it to 128 numbers.

State-of-the-art embeddings

We evaluated OlmoEarth v1.3's embeddings against AlphaEarth Foundations (AEF) and Tessera v2 across 27 evaluations, covering six continents and many different tasks. OlmoEarth’s 128-dimensional embeddings score highest on 20 of 27 evals and rank highest overall. The 64-dimensional version, at half the size, still leads on 18 of 27 evals. As part of this evaluation, we introduce PLANTEUR, a new crop-type benchmark for tropical farming, and the embeddings generalize best to places a classifier has never seen (PLANTEUR technical report is available here). Everything behind them is fully open: the model weights, the pretraining data, and the pretraining code.

In practice, this means a small classifier trained on the OlmoEarth embeddings is enough to map what’s on the ground: think classifying smallholder crops in Kenya, detecting brick kilns west of Dhaka, assessing fire damage in Indonesia, and tracking gold mining in the Peruvian Amazon.

Compared to previous generations of OlmoEarth models, OlmoEarth v1.3 was also our cheapest model to train. It took 53% of the computing time of our last version (v1.2) and 18% of our first (v1), with 50% and 22% of the carbon emissions. And it also remains a strong fine-tuning model, matching v1.2's performance across research and partner labels. Our latest model builds on the same foundation as earlier OlmoEarth versions, tuned so the embeddings stay lightweight without giving up accuracy across tasks, and that efficiency work carries forward into the versions ahead.

Full results and methodology are in our technical report.

If you wanted to reproduce it, pre-training OlmoEarth v1.3 Base would cost roughly $2,720 of rented H100 time for the final run. The weights, data, and code are all open.

One place, nine years

How much each pixel’s embedding changed between 2017 and 2020 (left) and 2020 and 2025 (right). Magenta is the largest change. Left: mining spreading southeast, the big patch at lower right. Right: that corner has gone quiet; the change now sits in the older mining zone to the west, part regrowth, part renewed digging. Explore it yourself in the OlmoEarth Embeddings Explorer.

In Peru's Madre de Dios region, illegal gold mining around La Pampa peaked in 2017 and 2018, clearing more than 1,200 hectares of forest in the buffer zone of the Tambopata National Reserve, according to Amazon Conservation's MAAP monitoring program. In February 2019, Peru's Operation Mercurio shut most of it down. The question ever since has been, did it stay down?

The embeddings help answer that. Compare each pixel's vector across years, no model training required, and the 2017 to 2020 pair lights up where the mining was spreading to the southeast. Run the same comparison from 2020 to 2025, and the signal shifts. The crackdown is visible in the embeddings.

The more interesting part is what the second map still shows. It is not dark. According to MAAP, pockets in the northwest kept operating, and the old mining zone keeps changing as the land recovers. The embeddings register that too. The reprieve was brief, and the pressure is building again. In August 2026, the Associated Press reported, Peru sent navy patrols back into the reserve after prosecutors found mining had crossed into Tambopata itself.

Our interactive story opens on this stretch of Madre de Dios, and walks through several other examples from there.

The OlmoEarth Embeddings Explorer

The OlmoEarth Embeddings Explorer is an interactive analysis tool built from the embeddings themselves, rendered as a false-color map of the planet. Pan anywhere, flip between years to see how landscapes have changed, and pull up the underlying Sentinel-2 imagery to check the map against the real thing. Then start asking questions: click a place to find others that look similar, or drop a few labeled points and train a small classifier on the spot, then export the result as a GeoTIFF. No account, no setup required.

For many teams, testing an idea against OlmoEarth has meant a fine-tuning run, on the order of hours. In the explorer, a first pass takes seconds. You can analyze entire regions from a handful of labels, no GPU needed. When a task calls for fine-tuning, the embeddings can help you decide whether it deserves the compute, and where the model falls short.

The archive behind the Explorer holds embeddings at 10-meter resolution, roughly 150 TB per year, covering land and adjacent coastal waters. At launch, 2025, 2024, and 2023 are global, and 2017 to 2022 cover select countries, with more coverage on the way. You can retrieve the embeddings in the full 128-dimensional version or the lighter 64-dimensional version. Every embedding also comes with a record of where it came from. For each 20-kilometer tile and year, open provenance tables list the Sentinel-1, Sentinel-2, and Landsat scenes the model read, with links to the public catalogs that host them, so you can trace any pixel back to the imagery behind it.

Get started

This release includes the OlmoEarth v1.3 Base model, the precomputed global embeddings, the OlmoEarth Embeddings Explorer, and the technical report. If your work needs a specific time window, OlmoEarth Studio runs the same model over the dates, modalities, and resolution that you choose, and a tutorial shows how to generate embeddings on your own compute. These tools work together: explore in the Embeddings Explorer, fine-tune in Studio when a task calls for it, and take your map from there. Everything is published under the OlmoEarth Artifact License, the same open license as v1 and v1.2.

Pull the embeddings for a place you care about, put your question to them, and show us what you find.

entries.title: Ensemble forecasting with IBM Granite time-series models
entries.content:
ibm-granite/granite-timeseries-ensemble-r1

Time Series Forecasting • Updated • 225 • 7

Ensemble forecasting with IBM Granite time-series models

Enterprise Article

Four open Granite models, one extensible forecasting interface, and less guesswork about which model to use.

Pre-trained time-series models can forecast without training on your dataset, but you still have to choose one. A model that handles smooth industrial signals well may struggle with noisy retail demand or a long seasonal horizon, and the best choice depends on the series and the task.

Granite Timeseries Ensemble reduces that choice to a sensible default. One recipe combines four complementary Granite architectures and returns median and quantile forecasts, with no retraining and no fitted ensemble weights. Start with the Probabilistic Ensemble (uniform probability pooling), compare the adaptive Inter Quartile Range (IQR) Ensemble, and extend the same interface with compatible forecasters. The ensemble recipe and its default Granite members are permissively licensed.

The idea will be familiar from weather forecasting. Ensemble forecasts explore a range of possible outcomes, and systems such as the North American Multi-Model Ensemble combine different models for seasonal prediction. Time-series forecasting benefits in a similar way: complementary models offer different views of what comes next, and an ensemble merges those views into one forecast.

Try Granite Timeseries Ensemble

Install Granite TSFM and load the recommended four-model recipe directly from Hugging Face:

pip install "granite-tsfm>=0.3.11"

import pandas as pd

from tsfm_public.models.ensemble.modeling_ensemble import QuantileEnsembleForecaster

df = pd.read_csv(
    "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/zhouhaoyi/ETDataset/main/ETT-small/ETTh1.csv",
    parse_dates=["date"],
)

ensemble = QuantileEnsembleForecaster.from_pretrained(
    "ibm-granite/granite-timeseries-ensemble-r1",
)

result = ensemble(
    df.tail(1024),
    timestamp_column="date",
    target_columns=["OT"],
    context_length=1024,
    prediction_length=24,
)

print(result.prediction_outputs) # point forecast
print(result.quantile_outputs)   # quantiles

The recipe stores the ensemble configuration rather than merged model weights. It downloads the four member checkpoints at runtime, so allow extra time for the first run. For the full configuration, member checkpoints, evaluation details, and limitations, see the model card.

result.prediction_outputs
contains the point forecast, while 
result.quantile_outputs
contains the quantile predictions which by default range from 0.1 to 0.9. Applications can use the point value as a central prediction and selected quantiles to express forecast ranges. For example, the 0.1 and 0.9 quantiles define a central forecast interval with nominal 80% coverage.

The ensemble members

The default recipe combines four pre-trained Granite models with different architectures:

ModelArchitecture
Granite PatchTST-FM-r1 Patched Transformer
Granite PatchTST-FM-r2 Patched Conformer
Granite FlowState-r1.1 State-space model
Granite TTM-r3 Tiny Time Mixers (MLP mixer)

For background, see the PatchTST-FM-r1 paper, PatchTST-FM-r2 architecture overview, FlowState paper, and Tiny Time Mixers paper.

These architectures capture trends, seasonality, and local variation in different ways, so their errors need not coincide. A 50-year review of forecast combinations describes how combining forecasts can reduce the risk of picking the wrong single model, while stressing that member quality and diversity still matter.

Two ways to combine the forecasts

Each member returns quantile forecasts. The two main recipes use different rules to turn those forecasts into one predictive distribution and its median.

Probabilistic Ensemble: the recommended default

The Probabilistic Ensemble (uniform probability pooling) gives each member equal influence, pools their quantile forecasts in probability space, and extracts the requested quantiles from the combined values. Because the weights are fixed, there is no fitting step and no weighting hyperparameters to tune for a new series.

The forecast combination puzzle offers useful motivation: in point forecasting, simple equal-weight combinations have often held up well against methods with estimated weights. This recipe applies the same equal-influence idea to probabilistic forecasts. It is the default loaded in the example above.

IQR Ensemble: an adaptive alternative

The IQR Ensemble weights members according to their forecast spread, giving narrower intervals greater influence. It approximates each member’s interquartile range from the closest available quantiles around the 25th and 75th percentiles. Weights vary by sample, target, and horizon step, and like the Probabilistic Ensemble, nothing is fitted from historical forecast errors. Isotonic regression keeps the combined quantiles from crossing.

A narrower interval does not necessarily mean a more accurate or better-calibrated forecast, and IQR weighting can favor an overconfident member. If you want to experiment, the recipe exposes a temperature setting (higher values move the weights toward uniform) and an optional cap on any single member's weight.

Load the evaluated IQR recipe by changing only the subfolder:

ensemble = QuantileEnsembleForecaster.from_pretrained(
    "ibm-granite/granite-timeseries-ensemble-r1",
    subfolder="recipes/granite-iqr",
)

Which method should I use?

Your goalStart withWhy
A simple defaultProbabilistic EnsembleEqual influence, no fitted weights
Adaptive weighting based on forecast spreadIQR EnsembleInfluence varies with each member's predicted spread

Start with the Probabilistic Ensemble. If forecast spread looks informative for your application, compare the IQR Ensemble against it on representative data, since accuracy and calibration depend on the series and the horizon.

Does the ensemble improve on its members?

We evaluated both recipes on 97 GIFT-Eval dataset configurations. The models forecast without fine-tuning, and test targets were not used to select or fit the aggregation method. Here we compare the official ensemble submission results with the four constituent models, using published leaderboard scores and ranks captured on 20 October 2026.

GIFT-Eval reports MASE for point forecasts and CRPS/MWQL (the benchmark's 

mean_weighted_sum_quantile_loss
metric) for probabilistic forecasts. Scores are normalized to Seasonal Naive and geometrically averaged across configurations. Lower is better.
ForecastMASE ↓MASE Rank ↓CRPS / MWQL ↓CRPS Rank ↓
Granite Ensemble R1 — Prob0.683★47.175★0.47150.948
Granite Ensemble R1 — IQR0.68448.7730.47147.619★
Granite PatchTST-FM-r20.68551.3710.467★48.918
Granite FlowState-r1.10.70166.4740.49069.485
Granite PatchTST-FM-r10.71774.7940.48868.134
Granite TTM-r30.72483.0620.52088.959

★ Best value among the forecasts shown. Lower is better.

Rank columns average per-configuration ranks against the full GIFT-Eval reference leaderboard, not just these six forecasts, so rank values can shift as entries are added to the leaderboard.

Both ensembles outperform all four individual members on aggregate MASE and average MASE Rank. The Probabilistic Ensemble achieves the lowest MASE among these six forecasts: 0.683 compared with 0.685 for PatchTST-FM-r2. Lower average MASE Rank indicates stronger relative point-forecast performance across GIFT-Eval’s diverse dataset configurations. Together, these results support the ensemble as a practical starting point, without requiring developers to select the strongest individual architecture in advance. The MASE margin over the best single member is small, so the main benefit is robustness: you get comparable or better aggregate accuracy without knowing in advance which architecture will suit your data.

PatchTST-FM-r2 retains the lowest aggregate CRPS/MWQL score. The IQR Ensemble achieves the lowest average CRPS Rank among these six forecasts, while the Probabilistic Ensemble ranks behind PatchTST-FM-r2 on that measure. Aggregate error and average rank therefore favor different choices.

In the 20 October 2026 comparison, the ensemble approach ranks 3rd among eligible systems on MASE Rank and CRPS Rank. The figure below shows both recipes alongside the ten best eligible reference systems per metric. Some systems, including entries excluded as fine-tuned or non-permissively licensed, score better than either recipe, so the value of the ensemble is not that it tops the leaderboard. It is that a single default delivers strong, consistent results across many series without requiring you to choose a member.

Figure: GIFT-Eval average-rank standings on 20 October 2026, showing both Granite ensembles alongside the ten best eligible reference systems per metric. Eligible systems have replication code and no declared test-data leakage; fine-tuned entries and systems with known non-permissive licenses or member dependencies are excluded. Rank values are taken directly from the published overall leaderboard snapshot; filtering changes which systems are displayed, not their rank values.

Extend the recipe to other forecasters

The default recipe uses four Granite models, but the common 

Forecaster
interface also accepts compatible external models. You can change the member mix or the aggregation method and keep the same downstream forecast format, with no merging or retraining of member checkpoints. That makes it easier to fit the ensemble into an existing forecasting stack, and to add forecasters suited to your domain as your needs evolve.

The repository also includes expanded recipes that add IBM Research checkpoints. These carry separate license terms, including non-commercial and research-use restrictions, so review each member's model card before using them.

For any new combination, check forecast compatibility, accuracy, calibration, latency, and licensing.

Evaluate the recipe for your application

GIFT-Eval is a broad benchmark, but aggregate gains don’t mean every series benefits, and average ranks don’t establish calibration. The way to find out how the recipes behave for your application is to backtest them on representative data:

  • Match your use case. Use historical forecast windows that reflect the data available at each forecast origin, the horizon you need, and the series you expect to serve.
  • Compare like with like. Run the Probabilistic Ensemble, the IQR Ensemble, and a strong individual member (such as PatchTST-FM-r2) on the same windows.
  • Look beyond point error. Assess quantile loss alongside MASE, and check the empirical coverage of the 0.1 to 0.9 interval against its nominal 80%.
  • Measure the cost. Record runtime and memory use to judge whether the benefit of combining four models justifies it for your workload.

Keep two limitations in mind. The current recipe forecasts multivariate channels independently, without using cross-channel information, and it loads four member checkpoints, which increases inference time and memory relative to a single member. Member context limits, horizons, preprocessing, and missing-value handling also differ, and neither aggregation method guarantees calibration or robustness under distribution shift, so keep monitoring forecasts after deployment.

Try it on your data

The recommended starting point is the default four-model recipe:

  • Granite Timeseries Ensemble on Hugging Face
  • Getting-started notebook
  • Granite TSFM repository
  • GIFT-Eval benchmark

Load the default recipe to get median and quantile forecasts from all four Granite architectures in one call, and adapt the recipe as your needs evolve.

References

  • ECMWF: Ensemble weather forecasting

  • NOAA: North American Multi-Model Ensemble

  • FlowState: Sampling-Rate-Equivariant Time-Series Forecasting

  • Tiny Time Mixers (TTMs): Fast Pre-trained Models for Enhanced Zero/Few-Shot Forecasting of Multivariate Time Series

  • Revisiting the Generic Transformer: Deconstructing a Strong Baseline for Time Series Foundation Models

  • Forecast combinations: an over 50-year review

  • Smith and Wallis (2009), A Simple Explanation of the Forecast Combination Puzzle

entries.title: NVIDIA Kumo Relational Outperforms Supervised Machine Learning on Relational Data, No Training Required
entries.content:
Enterprise + Article

TL;DR

NVIDIA Kumo Relational is a pre-trained relational foundation model that makes predictions directly on enterprise databases. Given a predictive query, it gathers up to 10,000 historical examples as context and predicts outcomes such as churn, demand, or fraud in a single forward pass. It needs no task-specific training, no feature engineering, and no flattening of tables. Kumo Relational is the first few-shot foundation model to outperform supervised machine learning on common relational benchmarks. Across 41 tasks on 15 databases, it beats supervised relational deep learning models and expert-engineered gradient-boosted tree pipelines, and on the SAP SALT enterprise benchmark it surpasses AutoGluon ensembles by 8% in mean reciprocal rank (MRR). It scales to databases with 500B+ rows and works for humans and agents alike, through NVIDIA's open-source, GPU-native structured-data-models library or as an NVIDIA NIM.

  • Paper: https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.12596
  • Documentation: https://docs.nvidia.com/sdgm/rfm/overview

The Shift to Structured Data Foundation Models

Foundation models have already rewritten the playbook for language and vision. Not long ago, production NLP meant a dedicated model per task, each fed by its own pipeline of tokenization, lemmatization, and n-grams. LLMs made that stack largely obsolete for three reasons: they were more accurate than the best task-specific models, far simpler to put into production, and flexible enough to open a new era of agentic applications.

The same shift is now underway for structured data. Relational databases power the world's most critical business decisions, yet predictive modeling on them still requires weeks of feature engineering, task-specific training, and tuned pipelines. Structured data foundation models change that for the same three reasons:

Better accuracy today: As drop-in replacements, these models already beat many production pipelines, especially XGBoost. On RelBench V1 classification tasks, Kumo Relational outperforms gradient-boosted trees on expert-engineered features by nearly 4 AUROC points on average. On SAP SALT, it beats XGBoost on engineered features by 7 MRR points out of the box and by 13 MRR points after fine-tuning. These results make a compelling case for replacing production XGBoost pipelines with Kumo Relational.

Simplicity and agility: One pre-trained model replaces separate pipelines for individual tasks. A new prediction becomes a query instead of a project, so ML teams can finally take on use cases that traditional ML made too laborious to build at every level of the organization.

Agents that can predict: LLMs let agents read, write, and reason. Structured data foundation models let them anticipate what happens next, such as which customer will churn, and act on it. Kumo Relational is already built to be called by agents, and its Predictive Query Language (PQL) gives them a simple interface for asking predictive questions.

Today, we are introducing Kumo Relational (paper, documentation), a pre-trained foundation model that brings this paradigm to relational data. Connect a database, describe what to predict, and get predictions in a single forward pass. No training required.

How Kumo Relational Works

Most foundation models for structured data operate on a single flat table. Real-world data lives in relational databases instead: users connected to orders connected to products, all evolving over time. Flattening these relationships into one row through manual aggregation (e.g., "average order value in the last 30 days") loses fine-grained structural signals and takes significant human effort.

Kumo Relational is a Relational Foundation Model that operates directly on the database, respecting its tables, foreign keys, and timestamps. It is pre-trained once on synthetic relational data that reflects real-world datasets and adapts to each new task through in-context learning, reading up to 10,000 context examples at inference time. Each example pairs a local subgraph around an entity at a point in time with its ground-truth target (e.g., "this user churned" or "this item sold 142 units").

![Overview of the NVIDIA Kumo Relational system: (a) database integration, (b) a prompting interface that turns natural language into a predictive query, and (c) automatic context generation feeding the NVIDIA Kumo Relational model, which scales horizontally across tenants.]

Figure 1. Overview of the Kumo Relational system. Connect a database, specify a predictive query, and Kumo Relational handles the rest, from context generation to model inference.

To make a prediction, Kumo Relational has to do three things: (1) understand the values within each table, (2) relate records across tables, and (3) relate context examples with known targets to the entity being predicted. Here is how it works:

![Kumo Relational architecture: (a) context input with task, users, orders and items tables; (b) column and row attention within tables with injected context targets; (c) graph attention and cross-sample attention across tables.]

Figure 2. Kumo Relational architecture: (a) context input, (b) reasoning within tables, (c) reasoning across tables.

Automatic Context Generation: Tasks are written in the Predictive Query Language (PQL), a declarative interface where you state what to predict rather than how. For temporal tasks, Kumo Relational replays historical database states: it samples entity-centric subgraphs up to an anchor timestamp and computes each target from events after that timestamp, while serving the model only the data from before it. This prevents data leakage.

Reasoning Within Tables: A lightweight network processes each table independently, alternating column attention (relating values within a column) and row attention (relating features within a row). The model learns which columns and rows matter for the current prediction and filters out noise before it propagates.

Reasoning Across Tables: A larger network distributes the row embeddings across the relational structure via graph attention over primary-key/foreign-key relationships, interleaved with cross-sample attention across context examples. This is where relational reasoning happens, such as linking a user's profile to their transaction history. Because this stage works on row embeddings rather than on every cell in every table, the design avoids quadratic cost and scales to large contexts and deeper subgraphs.

How Kumo Relational Was Built

Kumo Relational is pre-trained on entirely synthetic relational data simulated to reflect real-world relational databases with diverse predictive queries. Pre-training proceeds in stages, from single tables to increasingly complex relational structures.

The diverse relational databases needed for pre-training are rarely public, so synthetic data fills the gap. Kumo Relational's generator builds on the approach of PluRel (Kothapalli et al., ICML 2026), which extends single-table data generators to full relational databases. Members of the Kumo team helped develop PluRel and co-authored the original paper. PluRel generates each database in three stages: a schema, foreign-key links between rows that cluster as they do in real data, and column values from Structural Causal Models with temporal trends and cross-table dependencies. Generation is lightweight, so pre-training data is effectively unlimited, and the PluRel paper shows that pre-training loss follows a power law as synthetic databases are added, with gains that carry over to real databases.

Through this pre-training, the model learns to filter, correlate, and aggregate information across tables instead of relying on fixed aggregations. When maximum accuracy matters, Kumo Relational can also be fine-tuned on a specific dataset and task.

Performance

In this paper, we evaluated Kumo Relational on 41 benchmarks across 15 relational databases from RelBench V1 and V2, SAP SALT, and 4DBInfer, spanning e-commerce, medical, enterprise, social, and academic domains. None of these datasets were seen in pre-training. Kumo Relational outperforms the strongest supervised models in both classification and regression, including relational deep learning models and expert-engineered tabular ensembles. On the RelArena-α leaderboard, which compares relational models and systems on RelBench V1, it also sits on the accuracy-efficiency Pareto front out of the box:

![Scatter plot of the RelArena-α leaderboard: relative accuracy as Elo across tasks (y-axis) versus median inference time per 1,000 samples (x-axis, log scale). Kumo Relational sits on the Pareto front at about 17 seconds and Elo 1,842. The highest-scoring entry, rt-plurel, reaches Elo 1,878 at about 7,300 seconds, roughly 430 times slower. Every other foundation model, feature-engineering system, and supervised model scores lower and runs slower than Kumo Relational.]

Figure 3. RelArena-α leaderboard: Elo across tasks versus median inference time per 1,000 samples (log scale). Kumo Relational is about 430× faster than the highest-scoring entry at similar accuracy.

The paper also reports that on the SAP SALT enterprise benchmark, Kumo Relational surpasses large AutoGluon ensembles by 8% in mean reciprocal rank (MRR) and recent tabular foundation models by about 25%, and fine-tuning extends its lead over AutoGluon to 16%. It also holds up under hard conditions: it performs well with as little as 0.2% of the training data as context, stays stable when up to 75% of foreign-key links are removed, and barely degrades when many noisy columns are added.

Limitations

Kumo Relational performs best on data with meaningful relationships and temporal dynamics, such as user behavior over time. On tasks with very large training sets, task-specific supervised models may still edge out in-context predictions, which used at most 10,000 context examples in our benchmarks. Fine-tuning of the foundation model is designed for exactly this case. Predictive signals must also be reachable within a limited number of hops, so start with a focused query over a few relevant tables and expand the graph as needed.

Demo

Kumo Relational runs in-context learning natively over databases: in memory, through database and warehouse connectors, or through a custom graph engine that handles 500B+ rows via memory-mapped I/O at up to 5 GB/s. It is available in NVIDIA's newly released, GPU-native structured-data-models library, the same open-source library that powers our sister model, Kumo Tabular. The library downloads the weights from the Hugging Face Hub on first use, so you can load the model in a GPU-backed notebook and predict directly from it. The code below passes context examples, prediction entities, and their related tables to the model:

# pip install structured-data-models
import sdm

model = sdm.models.KumoRelational(device="cuda")
pred = model(
    # In-context training table (fkeys/timestamps/targets):
    x_context=...,
    y_context=...,
    # Prediction examples (fkeys/timestamps):
    x_query=...,
    # Multi-table information for context/prediction entities:
    related_context_tables=...,
    related_query_tables=...,
)

See the library's relational examples for complete RelBench and SAP SALT pipelines, including how to sample each entity's related tables.

To run the model as a separate service instead, deploy it as an NVIDIA NIM and point the open-source structured-data-models-client at it from your notebook. You write the prediction in PQL, and the client gathers the context examples and related tables, then sends the request:

# pip install 'structured-data-models-client[relational]'
import sdm_client

client = sdm_client.SDMClient(url="http://localhost:8001")  # NIM URL
query = sdm_client.PredictiveQuery(
    # Prediction task in Predictive Query Language (PQL):
    "PREDICT COUNT(orders.*, 0, 30, days) FOR EACH users.user_id",
    # Multi-table data as pandas DataFrames (keys/links inferred):
    {"users": ..., "orders": ...},
)
pred = client.predict(
    # Context examples and related tables for the entities to predict:
    query.materialize(indices=[1, 2, 3]),
    model=sdm_client.KumoRelational(),
)

See the client's example notebooks for end-to-end runs against a local NIM and on Databricks.

Start Building with NVIDIA Kumo Relational

NVIDIA Kumo Relational is available today. Read the research paper, explore the quickstart notebook, or start making predictions on your own data. The code is released under the Apache 2.0 license and the model weights under the OpenMDW License Agreement, version 1.1. NVIDIA believes Trustworthy AI is a shared responsibility, and we have established policies and practices to enable development for a wide array of AI applications. When downloaded or used in accordance with our terms of service, developers should work with their supporting model team to ensure this model meets requirements for the relevant industry and use case and addresses unforeseen product misuse. Please report model quality, risk, security vulnerabilities, or NVIDIA AI concerns here.

  • Paper: https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.12596
  • Documentation: https://docs.nvidia.com/sdgm/rfm/overview
  • Code: https://github.com/NVIDIA/structured-data-models
  • PyPI: https://pypi.org/project/structured-data-models/
  • Client code: https://github.com/NVIDIA/structured-data-models-client
  • Client PyPI: https://pypi.org/project/structured-data-models-client/
  • Weights: https://huggingface.co/nvidia/Kumo-Relational
  • Quickstart notebook: https://github.com/NVIDIA/structured-data-models-client/blob/main/examples/local/relational.ipynb
  • Related Research: Predictive Query Language (PQL), PluRel, Kumo Tabular

entries.title: How Specializing the Vocabulary of SLMs Can Cut Inference Cost by 77% in Real Applications
entries.content:
Team Article

Models specialized for a domain or a task by fine-tuning general open-source models, such as Qwen and Gemma, inherit a vocabulary built for many domains and general applications.

In an essay grader we run in production, that vocabulary split the text the model writes most into many tokens. This article previews some results from the VocabX paper, which we will publish soon: how we specialized the vocabulary around the cost of each token rather than its frequency, and cut measured inference cost by 77% without changing the base model.

The tokenizer is usually treated as a fixed property of the base model, inherited and left alone. For a model specialized in a single domain, it can be one of the largest cost levers, and it is set before any training step.

One of the systems we run in production is an automated grader for Portuguese essays, built on Qwen3-4B. It receives the essay, the prompt and the supporting texts, and returns a JSON assessment with a grade and a comment for each competency.

The model was already small, at 4 billion parameters, and had already been trained for the task. Its tokenizer, however, was still the original Qwen3-4B one, built for many languages and many kinds of text. In the grader, it was used for a single language, Portuguese, and a single response format. That had two costs: the text the grader writes on every request took more tokens than it needed, and at every generated token the model scored a vocabulary of 151,669 entries, including many this task almost never uses.

We rebuilt that vocabulary with a method we call VocabX, keeping the same base model, the same data and the same training recipe. The numbers in this article come from the current version of the paper, still under review, and may change before publication.

A Vocabulary Built for Everyone

The leading language models read and write in tokens, and the tokenizer decides how text becomes tokens. The tokenizers of the leading general-purpose models are trained on large collections of text from many domains and languages, from source code to contracts to Chinese. For a general-purpose model, that choice makes sense.

For a model used in a single domain, it creates two kinds of waste at once.

The first is fragmentation. The tokenizer splits into many pieces exactly what the domain repeats most. In the grader, every response starts with the same JSON envelope, the same competency names, the same evaluation phrases. In contracts, it is the boilerplate clauses. In code, the identifiers. Each of these sequences costs several tokens where one would do, and the model pays for every one of them on every request.

The second is excess. The vocabulary carries tens of thousands of entries the domain never uses, and the model computes a score for all of them at every token it generates. A model tuned to grade American school biology exams will almost never write in Chinese, yet it computes the probability of every Chinese-language token at every step. The vocabulary splits into many pieces what the domain repeats most, and carries entries the domain never uses.

Reading Is Cheap, Writing Is Expensive

The natural reaction is to count tokens and try to reduce the count. But the count is not the bill.

To see why a generated token costs more, it helps to look at how inference works. It has two phases. In prefill, the model processes the whole input in a single pass through the network: each weight read from GPU memory is reused for every input token, and the limit is compute. In decode, the model generates the response one token at a time, and each token needs a full pass. Each weight read is used only a few times, and the GPU spends most of its time waiting for data to arrive from memory: the limit becomes memory bandwidth.

This effect is strongest exactly where we operate: small models served with moderate batches. Batching requests splits the weight reads across them and eases the problem, but does not solve it. At every decode step, the model also reads the KV cache, the attention memory that holds the context already processed and grows with it. In the case we measured, the grader, a generated token costs 7.4 times a token read, but the ratio varies with the hardware, the problem, the batch size, the context length and other factors, and it can be larger than that. In general, the direction holds: generating costs more than reading.

Think of a shipping company that charges per box, but charges seven times more for outgoing boxes than for incoming ones. Reducing the total number of boxes helps. Reducing the outgoing boxes helps seven times more. A method that compresses input and output equally misses most of the possible savings.

The third component of the bill is the vocabulary itself. The model's last layer, the LM head, turns the internal state into a score for every possible token. To do that, it holds one row of parameters per vocabulary entry. In a model the size of Qwen3-4B, that matrix accounts for almost 10% of the parameters. It is a share that large models absorb without noticing, but it weighs on a small model.

And the cost is not paid only once. The input layer looks up only the row of the token being read, but the LM head reads and multiplies the entire matrix for every generated token. Since decode is already memory-bound, every extra row is more data to move at every step. An entry the domain never uses costs exactly the same as a frequent one. That is why adding tokens can lower the count and raise the bill at the same time. VocabX does not include this term in its selection criterion, but it controls vocabulary size in two steps: the sub-word merge replaces the base vocabulary with a smaller, domain-specific one, and macros enter under a fixed budget. In the grader, the output layer went from about 152,000 to about 65,000 rows.

Why Existing Solutions Fell Short

Adapting a model's vocabulary is not a new idea. Reference methods in the literature, such as fast vocabulary transfer (FVT), multi-word tokenization (MWT) and Liquid AI's in-place tokenizer expansion (in-place BPE), which continues BPE training from the original vocabulary, already reduce fragmentation. When we tested them on our problem, we found two limitations.

They choose tokens by frequency, not by cost. An expression that appears often in the input is worth more to them than one that appears less often in the response, even if the second is the more expensive one to serve.

They work on a single layer. They either adjust how words are cut into pieces, or merge whole phrases into one token. None of these three does both under the same criterion. And the grader's biggest waste was precisely in long, repeated spans such as the JSON envelope, which a sub-word method only reaches after merging each part, one by one.

How We Solved It

VocabX addresses both limitations, plus a third problem that appears on the obvious path to solving the first.

First, we changed the question. Instead of asking how many tokens a candidate saves, we ask how much cost and time it saves. Each eliminated token is multiplied by the price of the field it appears in: system prompt, user message or model response. In the case we measured, the grader, a token saved in the response is worth 7.4 times one saved in the input, and the vocabulary is built accordingly.

Second, we work on both layers at once. Back to the shipping company: you can cut boxes by packing each item better, or by recognizing that the same twelve-item kit ships every week and sending the kit in a single box. VocabX does both. At the sub-word layer, it rebuilds how domain words are cut into pieces. At the multi-word layer, it looks for whole spans that repeat, from short expressions to full lines and JSON envelopes, and turns each into a single token, which we call a macro token. Both layers are chosen under the same cost criterion, each with its own budget.

To find these spans, we use five miners, automatic searches for spans that repeat across the corpus, each specialized in one kind of repetition: long words, whole lines, expressions, complete sentences, and structures with punctuation such as JSON and tags. Averaged over eight corpora, the last one contributed the most, and on code it alone accounted for 17.5 points. Without all five, token reduction on the grader would drop by 55.6 points.

Third, we estimate what the sample cannot see. Choosing tokens by cost requires knowing how much each candidate still saves after the ones already chosen. Measuring that exactly would require reprocessing the entire corpus after every choice, tens of thousands of times. A common way to do this at scale is to measure on a sample of documents, and then a candidate absent from the sample gets zero gain.

An expression that appears 37 times in 50,000 documents shows up in a 400-document sample only about 26% of the time. In a contracts corpus, only 16.6% of the candidates appear in a 400-document sample; the rest are never evaluated.

A candidate's gain has two parts. One is how much it saves over the entire corpus, and that can be counted exactly, without a sample. The other is how much of that saving is not yet covered by the tokens already chosen, and only that part needs to be estimated. For candidates the sample cannot see, we use a statistical estimate based on the behavior of the ones it can see, instead of zero. A candidate that is rare in the sample but frequent in the corpus is back in the running.

That change alone, with the same sample and the same budget, raised token reduction on a contracts corpus from 44.7% to 52.8%.

What Changed in the Grader

To measure the real effect, we trained seven versions of the grader with the same base model, the same data, the same recipe and the same seed. The only difference between them is the tokenizer. All of them ran the same 500 requests on the same test machine, with an RTX 5090 GPU and the vLLM inference server, and cost was calculated from measured runtime.

The model's response dropped from 350 to 101 tokens on average. Cost dropped 77.0%. Quality, measured by the bench score, which combines grading accuracy and the accuracy of screening off-topic or rule-breaking essays, rose from 0.703 to 0.810.

Getting there required a course correction. The first version of the vocabulary fused each competency's grade with the surrounding JSON into a single macro token. It was the most compact option, but quality dropped: its bench score was 0.689, below the production grader's 0.703. With the grade inside the macro, each combination of grade and structure became a different variant of the same token, and the model chose both in a single step. Giving the grade its own token cost 2 extra tokens per response, raised the bench score to 0.810 and, in the measurement, was even cheaper: a 77.0% reduction, against 73.3% for the fused version.

The lesson applies beyond the grader. Compression has a cost when the compressed span carries the very decision the model exists to make. The goal is not the cheapest possible vocabulary, but the cheapest one that preserves the tokens that matter.

Beyond the Grader

To find out whether the gain was specific to our case, we compared VocabX with the three reference methods on five public domains (contracts, medical papers, scientific papers, news and Python code) and three model families (Qwen3, Llama-3.1 and Gemma-3). All methods used the same mining and test documents, and the same vocabulary ceiling.

VocabX compressed more than the strongest reference method in all fifteen combinations, by 1.2 to 9.3 points. In estimated inference cost, the pruned version of VocabX also led in all fifteen, with average margins of 10.2 points on Qwen3, 7.5 on Llama-3.1 and 13.6 on Gemma-3. On contracts, the pruned version reached 62.6% token reduction with 113,426 vocabulary entries, against 61.8% for the best in-place BPE configuration, which uses 207,803.

Paying Only for the Tokens That Matter

VocabX does not make the model smarter. It makes the model stop paying for text it does not need to write piece by piece, and stop scoring a vocabulary it will never use. In our grader, that cut measured inference cost by 77%, with the same base model and the same training recipe.

Specialization usually starts with data and weights. It can also start one layer earlier, in the vocabulary.

The full method, the tables for every experiment and the discarded interventions will be in the VocabX paper, which we will publish soon.

Sources

  • Dharma-AI. "VocabX: Cost-Weighted Vocabulary Adaptation for Domain-Specific Language Models." In preparation (2026).
  • Gee, Leonidas, et al. "Fast vocabulary transfer for language model compression." EMNLP Industry Track (2022).
  • Gee, Leonidas, et al. "Multi-word tokenization for sequence compression." EMNLP Industry Track (2023).
  • Smith, Jimmy T.H., et al. "In-Place Tokenizer Expansion for Pre-trained LLMs." arXiv:2607.15232 (2026).

Further Reading

entries.title: Profiling TorchNeuron (Part 1): System-level profiling on AWS Trainium.
entries.content:
jlongen-aws/blog-assets

Viewer • Updated • 1 • 312

Profiling TorchNeuron (Part 1): System-level profiling on AWS Trainium.

Enterprise Article

Many ML practitioners have some intuition about how to make models run fast, but fewer know how to analyze why a model is slow. In Part 1 of this series, you will learn how to systematically analyze inference performance and identify where the time is spent.

This post starts from scratch and assumes no prior profiling experience. The walkthrough uses AWS Trainium, a purpose-built AI chip for deep learning training and inference workloads, and TorchNeuron, its open source native PyTorch backend. TorchNeuron supports standard PyTorch workflows on Trainium, including eager execution, 

torch.compile
, and standard PyTorch APIs, with minimal code changes. Additionally, TorchNeuron integrates with Neuron Kernel Interface (NKI) to enable custom operators and performance optimization for Trainium hardware. By the end, you should know:
  • How to configure 
    torch.profiler
    with the Neuron backend and capture a clean trace.
  • How to read the 
    key_averages()
    table to identify which operations consume Neuron device time and compare their Self CPU time.
  • How to follow one operation through Neuron Explorer, from framework dispatch through runtime scheduling to hardware execution on a NeuronCore.
  • How these signals change across three implementations of the same operation.

Neuron as a PyTorch Backend

Before you profile a workload, it helps to understand how Neuron integrates with PyTorch.

The Neuron backend uses PyTorch's 

PrivateUse1
extension point. This mechanism lets an accelerator integrate with the framework without adding a dedicated dispatch key such as 
cuda
. The 
torch_neuronx
package works with upstream PyTorch to register Neuron as a native backend for PyTorch code. For details about this extension mechanism, see Facilitating New Backend Integration by PrivateUse1.

Set Up the Profiler

You use two objects to profile a Neuron workload:

  • NeuronConfig
    controls which Neuron data streams and NeuronCores to capture and where to write the output. You pass it to 
    torch.profiler.profile
    as 
    experimental_config
    .
  • NeuronProfiler
    takes a 
    NeuronConfig
    and provides an 
    export_trace
    callback. The callback writes the framework trace, 
    trace.json
    , alongside the Neuron system traces.
nc = NeuronConfig(
    modes=[ProfileMode.DEVICE, ProfileMode.RUNTIME],
    profile_output_dir=OUTPUT_DIR,
    capture_enabled_for_nc='0',
    correlate_device_time=True,
)
exporter = NeuronProfiler(nc)

The 

modes
parameter selects the data streams to capture, such as device instructions and runtime traces. The 
capture_enabled_for_nc
parameter selects the NeuronCores to trace. Setting 
correlate_device_time=True
propagates device time from the trace into the 
key_averages()
table, where you can compare CPU and Neuron device time. For the complete parameter reference and available 
ProfileMode
values, see the NeuronConfig Profile Modes documentation.

Tooling: Neuron Explorer

Neuron Explorer is a browser-based viewer for the system trace, device timeline, and per-engine breakdown. You can access it through an SSH tunnel or the Visual Studio Code extension. In this post, you use Explorer to confirm what 

key_averages()
reports numerically and inspect what happens between dispatches.

After profiling, the output directory contains the system trace and, when you capture device data, matched 

.neff
and 
.ntff
files. The Neuron Executable File Format (NEFF) contains the compiled Neuron executable, while the matching NTFF contains its hardware instruction trace. The files share a numeric hash that identifies them as a pair. To open the profile in Neuron Explorer, upload the complete output directory for a system or combined profile. For a device-only profile, upload the matching 
.neff
and 
.ntff
files individually. See Step 5: Upload your profile for the UI and command-line instructions.

Profile RMSNorm

For this first analysis, you profile RMSNorm, a small operation with a clear sequence of arithmetic and reduction operations.

You profile three implementations of the same operation:

  • Naive RMSNorm with individual PyTorch operations: multiply, mean, add, reciprocal square root, and multiply.
  • torch.rms_norm()
    , the PyTorch built-in lowered to a single fused Neuron kernel.
  • Naive RMSNorm with 
    torch.compile
    , using the same operations as the first implementation.

The scripts use the same inputs, profiler configuration, and schedule so the results are directly comparable.

All scripts to reproduce this work are available in the 

torch-neuronx
examples directory.

Profile 1: Naive PyTorch Operations

Start by writing RMSNorm with individual PyTorch operations. Each line maps to one or more ATen operations and can create intermediate tensors.

device = torch.device('neuron')

x = torch.randn(4, 512, dtype=torch.bfloat16, device=device)
weight = torch.ones(512, dtype=torch.bfloat16, device=device)

def rms_norm_fn(t):
    x_sq = t * t                                    # square
    mean_sq = x_sq.mean(dim=-1, keepdim=True)       # mean of squares
    rms = torch.rsqrt(mean_sq + 1e-6)               # 1 / sqrt(mean_sq + eps)
    return t * rms * weight                         # normalize + scale

Call the profiler with two arguments required for the Neuron backend:

  • Include 
    ProfilerActivity.PrivateUse1
    to collect activity from the Neuron device.
  • Pass 
    NeuronConfig
    as 
    experimental_config
    to enable the Neuron-specific Kineto features.

The schedule uses 

wait=2
, 
warmup=1
, and 
active=1
across four 
prof.step()
calls. This records one warm iteration without including initial setup overhead.

Call 

torch.neuron.synchronize()
inside the profiler loop. Without this synchronization, the profiler can export before the device finishes and leave the Neuron time column empty.
with torch.profiler.profile(
    activities=[ProfilerActivity.CPU, ProfilerActivity.PrivateUse1],
    experimental_config=nc,
    record_shapes=False,
    schedule=torch.profiler.schedule(wait=2, warmup=1, active=1),
) as prof:
    for step in range(4):
        with torch.no_grad():
            _ = rms_norm_fn(x)
        torch.neuron.synchronize()
        prof.step()

After profiling finishes, inspect the 

key_averages()
table. Sort by 
self_privateuse1_time_total
to place the operations with the highest device cost first. The table shown here is filtered to the RMSNorm operations that report Neuron device time. The full 
key_averages()
output also includes CPU-side events such as allocations and host-to-device transfers.
print(prof.key_averages().table(sort_by="self_privateuse1_time_total", row_limit=4))

The key averages table shows that three aten::mul calls account for the largest share of Neuron device time.

The table shows which ATen operations ran, how often they ran, and how much time they spent on the CPU and Neuron device. 

aten::mul
has the highest total device time because the function performs three multiplications.
Name# CallsSelf CPUSelf NEURON% NEURON
aten::mul360.9 μs1,164.5 μs49.5%
aten::add126.6 μs434.6 μs18.5%
aten::rsqrt115.6 μs415.0 μs17.6%
aten::mean121.1 μs340.8 μs14.5%

Self NEURON total: 2.355 ms

Each row maps directly to the function. 

aten::mul
runs for 
x * x
, 
x * rms
, and the final multiplication by 
weight
. 
aten::mean
reduces the last dimension. 
aten::add
adds the epsilon value and triggers a host-to-device copy because the scalar starts on the CPU. 
aten::rsqrt
computes the reciprocal square root.

Neuron Explorer follows an aten::mul operation from framework dispatch through runtime scheduling to execution on the Neuron hardware lanes.

Read the Trace in Explorer

In Explorer, time flows from left to right and the event lifecycle flows from top to bottom. Each ATen operation follows the same pattern: creation in the framework lane, scheduling in the runtime lane as 

nrta_execute_schedule
, and device execution in the hardware lane as 
nc_exec_running
.

The system trace view organizes events into lanes. In the Default grouping mode, labels follow the pattern instance/PID/subsystem/identifier:

LaneLabel suffixWhat it shows
Framework dispatch
framework/TID:
 Operator dispatch events (PrivateUse1 runtime), grouped by thread ID.
Framework device
framework/Stream:
 Device interaction events (PrivateUse1 driver), grouped by stream number.
Neuron Runtime
neuron_rt/NC:
 Neuron Runtime API calls, grouped by logical NeuronCore.
Neuron Hardware
neuron_hw/NC:
 Hardware execution events, grouped by physical NeuronCore.

In eager mode, each operation runs independently. Use the dependency chain viewer to follow 

aten::mul.Tensor
from the framework layer through runtime scheduling to device execution.

The dependency chain viewer highlights the lifecycle of one operation across the framework, runtime, and hardware lanes.

Profile 2: torch.rms_norm

Replace the individual operations with PyTorch's built-in 

rms_norm
function. Neuron lowers the operation to one fused kernel:
def rms_norm_fn(t):
    return torch.rms_norm(t, [512], weight)

The fused RMSNorm appears as one device operation in the key averages table.

Name# CallsSelf CPUSelf NEURON% NEURON
aten::_fused_rms_norm147.6 μs403.3 μs100%

Self NEURON total: 403.3 μs

The fused RMSNorm follows one framework-to-hardware path instead of dispatching each arithmetic operation separately.

Compare the Lowering Path

In the naive implementation, each operation crosses the dispatch boundary independently and follows its own framework-to-runtime-to-hardware path. In the fused implementation, one Python call covers the complete computation. The trace contains one dispatch and one hardware event, with no gaps between component operations.

Profile 3: Naive PyTorch with torch.compile

For the final example, compile the original naive RMSNorm function with 

torch.compile
.

With 

@torch.compile(backend="neuron")
, TorchDynamo captures the Python bytecode as an FX graph and AOTAutograd lowers it to ATen operations. The Neuron backend receives the complete graph instead of dispatching each operation separately. It fuses the operations, optimizes memory access, and compiles the graph into a single NEFF artifact. The artifact runs as one hardware dispatch.
@torch.compile(backend='neuron', fullgraph=True)
def naive_compiled(t):
    x_sq = t * t
    mean_sq = x_sq.mean(dim=-1, keepdim=True)
    rms = torch.rsqrt(mean_sq + 1e-6)
    return t * rms * weight

The compiled function appears as one Torch-Compiled Region in the key averages table.

Name# CallsSelf CPUSelf NEURON% NEURON
Torch-Compiled Region: 0/0198.4 μs375.5 μs100%

Self NEURON total: 375.5 μs

The compiled graph follows one path through runtime scheduling and hardware execution.

The table shows one device execution, as in Profile 2, but the code takes a different path. Instead of calling a purpose-built fused operation, the compiler discovers the fusion from the original Python function. In this run, the Neuron time is comparable to 

torch.rms_norm
, at 375 μs compared with 403 μs.

Side-by-Side Summary

VariantNEURON timeSelf CPU timeOperator calls
Naive ops2,355 µs~125 µs6
torch.rms_norm403 µs~48 µs1
Naive + torch.compile376 µs~98 µs1

Both 

torch.rms_norm
and 
torch.compile
fuse RMSNorm into one kernel dispatch. In these runs, either approach takes about one-sixth of the naive implementation's device time. Fusion removes the gaps between hardware executions and avoids materializing intermediate values such as 
x_sq
and 
mean_sq
between separately dispatched operations.

Conclusion 

key_averages()
shows which operations consume device time, while its full output also reveals CPU-side setup and transfers. Explorer provides the corresponding visual trace. You can follow one operation from framework dispatch through runtime scheduling to hardware execution and see the gaps that fusion removes.

You can use the same workflow on larger models: find a hotspot in the table, verify it in the trace, and then determine whether a fused operation or 

torch.compile
can reduce its cost.

In Part 2, we will move into the device-level profile. You open the NEFF, inspect the TensorEngine, VectorEngine, and direct memory access (DMA) breakdown, and place the kernel on the roofline to determine whether it is compute-bound or memory-bound.

Special thanks to Aritra Roy Gosthipaty for the inspiration to begin this series, and to my peers Pinak Panigrahi, Samir Araujo, Akhil Azhikodan, Esha Lakhotia and the rest for reviewing!

Automatic Speech Recognition • 2B • Updated • 34.8k • 101

Granite Speech 5.0: Transcribe, Translate, and Attribute more Accurately and Faster

Enterprise Article

We're excited to share three updates to IBM's Granite Speech collection: a new speech-language model, granite-speech-5.0-2b, and revised versions of two models the community already uses, granite-speech-5.0-470m-turboctc and granite-speech-4.1-2b-plus. Together they cover the full range of enterprise speech work: transcription and translation with high accuracy, extremely fast transcription at the edge, and recordings where who spoke, and when, matter as much as what was said.

ModelStatusWhat's newBest for
granite-speech-5.0-2b
 NewMore accurate, noise- and reverb-robust automatic speech recognition (ASR), language-ID prompting, 2,000-term keyword biasing, better long-form translationHigh-accuracy multilingual transcription and translation
granite-speech-5.0-470m-turboctc
 UpdatedMultilingual, native punctuation and capitalization, and more robust to noise and reverbHigh-throughput and on-device transcription
granite-speech-4.1-2b-plus
 UpdatedImproved speaker attribution, timestamps, keyword biasing, and long-speech performanceMeetings, calls, and other multi-speaker recordings

Granite Speech 5.0 2B: more accurate, more robust, more control 

granite-speech-5.0-2b
is the successor to 
granite-speech-4.1-2b
at the same parameter count. It transcribes English, French, German, Spanish, Portuguese, and Japanese, and translates to and from English in those languages, plus English to Italian and Mandarin. It was trained on 390,000 hours of public audio, plus synthetic data built for Japanese ASR, keyword biasing, and translation.

What's new compared with 4.1 2B Speech:

  • More accurate, more robust English ASR: Higher accuracy on English short-form benchmarks, and better handling of noise, reverberation, and distant-microphone speech.
  • Language ID prompting: Name the input language in the prompt to steer multilingual transcription.
  • Better long-form and conversational translation: Translation holds up for longer with more natural speech, not just short read sentences.
  • Keyword lists up to 2,000 terms: Bias transcription and translation toward product names, people, and acronyms, in every supported language.
  • Punctuation and capitalization on request: Ask for formatted output in the prompt; capitalization F1 ranges from 89.7 to 99.5 across our test sets.

The model ships under Apache 2.0 with support in Transformers, vLLM, llama.cpp, and mlx-audio for Apple Silicon.

Chart 1: granite-speech-5.0-2b ranks #2 among top open-weight ASR models on average English WER (5.06%). Lower is better. Results are official, as of 21 October 2026, and averaged over the Open ASR Leaderboard’s public English short-form test sets.

Granite Speech 5.0 Turbo CTC: now multilingual, more robust, and even faster

When we introduced Turbo CTC in August, it was an English-only, 470M-parameter encoder built for speed. This revision keeps that footprint and adds the three things users asked for most:

  • Multilingual transcription: English, Japanese, Spanish, German, French, Italian, and Portuguese.
  • Native punctuation and capitalization: Transcripts come out ready to read, with no separate punctuation or truecasing step.
  • More robust in difficult acoustics: Training that explicitly targets reverberant audio makes Turbo CTC more robust in echoey rooms and far-field recordings.

It's also faster. By compiling a single Conformer block and reusing its graph across the stack, we cut warmup time and pushed Turbo CTC to 19,870 RTFx on the Open ASR Leaderboard, up from roughly 12,600 RTFx at launch: about 1.6x faster, at the same accuracy level.

Chart 2: Average WER vs. RTFx on the Open ASR Leaderboard (English short-form, 9 public test sets, as of October 2026). Lower WER and higher RTFx are better; RTFx is on a log scale.

Granite Speech 4.1 2B Plus: better at who said what, and when

The updated 

granite-speech-4.1-2b-plus
is tuned for the recordings enterprises actually have: meetings, support calls, and interviews with several speakers running long. It keeps the 4.1 name because the architecture, prompt format, and API are unchanged, so it's a drop-in replacement for the current model with improved weights. This revision improves four areas:
  • Speaker attribution: More accurate labeling of who is speaking. Word diarization error rate (WDER) drops 7%, and speaker-attributed WER (cpWER) drops 7% overall.
  • Timestamps: Average timestamp shift (AAS) is cut by more than half, yielding tighter timing in captions, search, and review.
  • Long-speech performance: WER on long-form test sets drops 24%.
  • Keyword biasing: Errors on biased keywords fall 45% with 20-term keyword lists.

Speaker-attributed transcriptscpWER30.5028.48

Table 1: All metrics are error rates, so lower is better. For more detailed results, see the model card.

Get started

Not sure which model to pick? Start here:

  • Need high transcription accuracy, translation, or keyword biasing? Use granite-speech-5.0-2b.
  • Need raw speed or on-device transcription? Use granite-speech-5.0-470m-turboctc, and try it in the browser with our WebGPU streaming demo.
  • Working with meetings or multi-speaker calls? Use granite-speech-4.1-2b-plus.
