We recommend pairing them with Granite Guardian for production deployments that need additional risk detection.

Give them a try and let us know what you think!

entries.title: Hugging Face ❤️ TorchTPU: TPUs, Natively
entries.content:
Update on GitHub

If you ever tried to run PyTorch on a TPU, you probably ported your code to 

torch_xla
, or you ended up having to learn JAX. With TorchTPU, a native PyTorch backend, TPU is now just another device. It opens up native support of TPU in the Hugging Face ecosystem. Transformers, Diffusers and Kernels run natively on TPU. Pick a model from the Hub, send it to 
"tpu"
, and you're done.

Wait, what's a TPU? 🤔

TPU stands for Tensor Processing Unit. TPUs are Google's own AI accelerators. They are chips built for one job: the matrix math that neural networks spend most of their time on. Google has been designing them for about ten years, and uses them to train and serve its own models, including Gemini.

TPUs are available on Google Cloud, from a single chip up to pods of thousands of chips. They shine when you need a lot of compute, for training or for serving at scale.

The catch has always been software. The TPU stack grew up around TensorFlow and JAX, and PyTorch users had to work harder to get in.

The old way

Until now, running PyTorch on TPUs meant going through PyTorch/XLA (

torch_xla
). It worked, but it had its quirks. Tensors were lazy (the tensors, not you), so your code didn't always run when you thought it did. Small changes could trigger graph recompilations, and debugging was hard to reason about.

To make life easier, we built Optimum TPU. It gave Hugging Face models inference and training support on TPUs. Now that TorchTPU brings native support, Optimum TPU is not required anymore to run Hugging Face models with Transformers and Diffusers.

Enter TorchTPU 🚀

TorchTPU adds TPU as a new backend to PyTorch. You write regular PyTorch code. It comes with Pallas kernels tuned for TPUs, support for distributed training, and a 

torch.compile
integration for when you want more speed. Installing it on a TPU VM takes one command:
pip install torch-tpu --extra-index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cpu

The extra index gives you the CPU build of 

torch
. Without it, pip pulls the much bigger CUDA build, which you don't need on a TPU.

Your favourite libraries, now on TPU

Transformers

Transformers v5 was built around one idea: be the source of truth for model definitions, so they can run anywhere. "Anywhere" now includes TPUs. To load a model on a TPU, pass 

device_map="tpu"
. That's it.
from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM, AutoTokenizer

model_id = "Qwen/Qwen3.5-9B"
model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(
    model_id,
    device_map="tpu", # will load model directly on the TPU
)
tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(model_id)
inputs = tokenizer("The future of AI is", return_tensors="pt").to("tpu")
out = model.generate(**inputs, max_new_tokens=64)
print(tokenizer.decode(out[0], skip_special_tokens=True))

The model runs in eager mode by default. You can also use 

torch.compile
for better performance, or run it in a distributed setup.

Images? Videos? Diffusers paints them on TPUs 🎨

TPU is now a first-class device in Diffusers. For prototyping or debugging, eager mode only needs 

pipe.to("tpu")
. For deployment, compiled mode adds one 
compile
call. Your pipelines and code stay the same, and there's no TPU fork to maintain.
import torch
from diffusers import StableDiffusion3Pipeline

pipe = StableDiffusion3Pipeline.from_pretrained(
    "stabilityai/stable-diffusion-3.5-medium", dtype=torch.bfloat16
)
pipe.to("tpu")  # eager mode: that's the whole change
# optional: compiled mode
pipe.transformer.compile(backend="tpu", fullgraph=True, dynamic=False)

image = pipe("a corgi astronaut planting a flag on a pizza moon").images[0]

The first call compiles, and every call after that with the same image size reuses the graph.

Models too big for one chip? Pass a 

TensorParallelConfig
to 
from_pretrained
and the transformer is sharded across chips as it loads, so the full model never has to fit in one place. Many popular pipelines support it out of the box, and the ones that don't are just a 
tp_plan
away. The Diffusers TPU guide has the full recipe.

Here are some examples run on a Cloud TPU v6e-4:

TP=4 (each model split across four chips) · bf16 · batch 1

MiniMax-H3 (video + audio) Qwen-Image-2.1
"The fluffy plush Hugging Face mascot from the picture, a round yellow smiling face with rosy cheeks and two little open hands, stands at the prow of an ancient Greek trireme […] Sound of crashing waves, creaking timber, wind in the rigging, distant seagulls, and a low epic orchestral swell." · 1344×768, 5.2 s, 49 steps · 188 s compiled, 262 s eager"A capybara wearing a wizard hat, reading a book by candlelight, oil painting" · 1024×1024, 40 steps · 3.5 s compiled, 8.0 s eager"A neon shop sign that reads 'QWEN IMAGE 2.1', rainy night, reflections on wet pavement" · 2048×2048, 40 steps

Kernels

The Kernels Hub has ready-to-use TPU kernels. Load one with the Kernels library and give your model a speed boost.

TPU kernels are written in Pallas, which gives you low-level control over the hardware. You can also bring in kernels from the Tokamax library. Here is a ragged-dot kernel from Tokamax plugged into a Mixture-of-Experts model:

from kernels import get_kernel
from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM
from transformers.integrations.moe import ALL_EXPERTS_FUNCTIONS

repo_id = "tengomucho/ragged-dot-tpu"
kernel = get_kernel(repo_id, version=1, trust_remote_code=[repo_id])
ALL_EXPERTS_FUNCTIONS.register("tokamax_ragged_dot", kernel.experts_forward)
model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(
    "Qwen/Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507",
    experts_implementation="tokamax_ragged_dot",
)

The bigger the batch, the bigger the win. At batch size 64, decoding is 21.5× faster on Qwen3-30B-A3B and 12.8× faster on Gemma 4 26B-A4B.

Decode throughput on a TPU v6e-8, Hub kernel vs. the default implementation.

We test it so you don't have to 🧪

We're continuously improving TPU support in transformers by running the library test suite. We are working to add a nightly CI on TPU and make the results available in the (transformers dashboard)[https://huggingface.co/spaces/transformers-community/transformers-ci-dashboard].

The Transformers CI dashboard, with TPU results next to other accelerators. Work in progress!

It's not all green yet, and we're fine with that. Of the tests that run on TPU, 96.5% pass. Every failure we find becomes a small repro script and an issue on the TorchTPU repo. So far we have reported 34 issues, and 19 are already fixed. Running on TPU also caught a few bugs in Transformers itself, like in 

StaticCache
and the Qwen3 tensor-parallel plans. We fixed those upstream.

If something breaks on TPU, we want to find out before you do.

Get started

TPUs are no longer a side quest for PyTorch users. Install TorchTPU, grab a model from the Hub, and send it to 

"tpu"
.

We can't wait to see what you build 🤗. If you hit a problem, open an issue and tell us about it.

entries.title: AnyLanguageModel 1.0: One Year of Local Models on Apple Platforms
entries.content:
LiquidAI/LFM2.5-2.6B-GGUF

Text Generation • 3B • Updated • 682k • 388

AnyLanguageModel 1.0: One Year of Local Models on Apple Platforms

Update on GitHub

Last November, we introduced AnyLanguageModel on this blog: a drop-in replacement for Apple's Foundation Models framework that lets you choose the model and provider your app uses. We heard from app developers who were curious about local models but weren't always sure how to get started. They also wanted to avoid the added complexity of supporting multiple inference providers. AnyLanguageModel grew out of that feedback.

Local and hosted inference each have their strengths, and both have a role in building this new generation of intelligent apps. A shared API makes it easier to choose the right model for each task.

A year and dozens of releases later, AnyLanguageModel 1.0 is out, along with swift-huggingface 1.0 and swift-xet 1.0.

Here's what changed, and what's next:

A drop-in compatible API

The core idea of AnyLanguageModel remains the same: use the Foundation Models API with the model that fits your app. To get started, change your 

import
statement:
- import FoundationModels
+ import AnyLanguageModel

The same session code then works with the system model, with open-weight models through llama.cpp, MLX, and Core ML, and with the hosted providers below.

Over the past year, we've added several major features:

  • Tool calling works with every provider.
  • Guided generation works with every provider, too, including nested 
    @Generable
    types and arrays of them.
  • Image support lets you attach images to prompts using Foundation Models 27's syntax, including when you use the system model on iOS, macOS, and visionOS 27.

On OS 27, AnyLanguageModel also works with any model that conforms to Foundation Models' 

LanguageModel
protocol, including Core AI models.

Alongside AnyLanguageModel, we've built out swift-huggingface and swift-xet to bring accelerated model downloads from the Hub to Swift apps.

Hosted models, too

Support for hosted models expanded this year, too. AnyLanguageModel now supports:

  • OpenAI's Chat Completions and Responses APIs
  • Open Responses, for any provider with a compatible endpoint
  • Anthropic's Messages API, with adaptive thinking and effort options
  • Google's Gemini API
  • Ollama
  • Private Cloud Compute, on OS 27
  • Hugging Face Inference Providers, and other OpenAI-compatible endpoints such as OpenRouter, through a custom base URL

With Inference Providers, you can use open-weight models that are too big to run on the device with the same session code:

let model = OpenAILanguageModel(
    baseURL: URL(string: "https://router.huggingface.co/v1/")!,
    apiKey: ProcessInfo.processInfo.environment["HF_TOKEN"]!,
    model: "openai/gpt-oss-120b",
    apiVariant: .chatCompletions
)

Hosted providers get the same features as local models: guided generation, tool calling with streaming, and token usage on responses.

Reasoning is now part of the transcript too. When you switch providers, reasoning blocks are automatically omitted from requests if the new provider can't replay them.

API keys come from a closure instead of a string, so your app can fetch short-lived tokens from your own server. The README explains when to let people bring their own keys and when to route requests through a proxy.

AnyLanguageModel also runs on Linux, so the same code can work on a server.

Open-weight models got better

While we've made local models easier to use, the models themselves have become more capable, making the small ones a good place to start. Here are some of the most downloaded models on the Hub right now:

  • Gemma 4 E2B from Google, in GGUF, about 3.4 GB at 
    Q4_0
    with quantization-aware training.
  • LFM2.5 2.6B from Liquid AI, in GGUF, about 1.7 GB at 
    Q4_K_M
    .
  • Qwen3.8 27B for MLX from Alibaba, about 16 GB at 4 bits.

The first two fit on an iPhone, and Qwen3.8 27B runs on a Mac with 32 GB of memory or more. Selecting the MLX model takes one line:

let model = MLXLanguageModel(modelId: "mlx-community/Qwen3.8-27B-4bit")

And if you have four maxed-out Mac Studios handy, GLM-5.3 from Z.ai takes about 1.5 TB in BF16. For the rest of us, it's available through Inference Providers.

Upgrading to 1.0 

dependencies: [
    .package(
        url: "https://github.com/huggingface/AnyLanguageModel",
        from: "1.0.0",
        traits: ["MLX"]
    )
]

If you're upgrading an existing app, see the migration guidance in the AnyLanguageModel, swift-huggingface, and swift-xet release notes for help updating your code.

Community feedback and contributions have shaped several of our major features. Thank you to everyone who contributed for helping make AnyLanguageModel more useful to app developers.

What's next

Language models have proven to be a powerful tool for building intelligence into products. They're also one of many kinds of models developers can put to work. We're excited to bring the same approach to more capabilities: familiar Swift APIs with a choice of models running on the device. Coming soon: models that decide, and models that listen.

entries.title: MPS in PyTorch 2.15
entries.content:
Update on GitHub

If you run models on your Mac or use MPS as your primary acceleration tool for computing, there's plenty to look forward to in PyTorch 2.15! FP8 arrives on MPS, language-model decoding gets faster paths through linear layers and softmax and new Metal kernels tackle some surprisingly expensive parts of audio, video and training workloads.

A quick word about who we are: we're the PyTorch team at Hugging Face. We contribute across PyTorch, and one of our focus areas is the MPS backend, where the goal is to make your Mac a first-class place to run and train PyTorch models. At the start of 2026, running even small models on MPS often meant working around unsupported operations, performance cliffs and unexpected memory growth. So we run real models from the Hugging Face Hub across language, image and video, find where MPS falls short and fix it upstream in PyTorch, more and more often by replacing MPSGraph with dedicated Metal kernels. Much of this post is the result of that work, done together with the PyTorch maintainers and community contributors.

TL;DR

  • FP8 comes to the Mac: store 
    float8_e4m3fn
    values in half the space of BF16 and use scaled matrix multiplication and all other ops which are supported on CUDA/CPU!
  • MoE models decode 5–6.5× faster than in 2.14: Qwen3.6-35B-A3B goes from 9.4 to 61.3 tokens/s on an M3 Ultra, thanks to a native grouped matmul with a dedicated decoding path, fewer GPU-CPU syncs and faster top-k routing.
  • Less time per token for every LLM: single-row linear layers use specialized matrix-vector kernels, and softmax over the vocabulary is about 8× faster.
  • More linear algebra on the GPU: complex LU and triangular solves, faster small-matrix inverses, and faster QR decomposition.
  • Audio, video, and training get attention too: faster paths for convolutions, padding, dropout, interpolation backward and reductions. Wan2.2's video VAE decode now peaks at 8 GiB of memory instead of 270 GiB.
  • More control from Python: public MPS streams and more reliable event timing.
  • Updated requirements: MPS now requires macOS 15 or later; PyTorch 2.15 requires Python 3.11 or later.
  • A peek at 2.16: attention fully on Metal, more MPSGraph-to-Metal migrations and faster LLM decoding.

What this means for you

If you run models on a Mac with transformers, diffusers or tools like ComfyUI, here's what 2.15 changes in practice:

  • Much faster local LLMs. Mixture-of-experts models decode 5–6.5× faster than in 2.14: on an M3 Ultra with 
    torch.compile
    , Qwen3.6-35B-A3B goes from 9.4 to 61.3 tokens/s and LFM2.5-8B-A1B from 23.6 to 123.6 tokens/s. Dense models benefit too, from faster linear layers and an 8× faster softmax for sampling. (More)
  • Video generation that fits in memory. Decoding a video with Wan2.2's tiled VAE used to push driver memory to 270 GiB; it now peaks at about 8 GiB. (More)
  • Correct image editing with Qwen-Image-2.1. On 2.14, the Qwen-Image-2.1 VAE encoder silently corrupted images on MPS, breaking image-edit workflows (reported in ComfyUI). The same padding change fixes it: an encode-decode round trip now matches CPU at 29.95 dB PSNR, up from 10.06 dB.
  • FP8 weights on your Mac. FP8 tensors take half the memory of BF16, and 
    F.scaled_mm
    multiplies them directly on the GPU. (More)

Contents

Getting started

You'll need an Apple silicon Mac with macOS 15 or later and Python 3.11 or later (see the 2.15 compatibility matrix). If your OS is too old or no Metal GPU is available, the MPS availability check now tells you why.

To try the release candidate in a separate environment:

uv pip install torch==2.15.0 --index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/test/cpu

FP8 comes to MPS

FP8 gives you another way to save memory on your Mac. PyTorch 2.15 adds 

torch.float8_e4m3fn
tensors on MPS: one byte per value, half the storage of FP16 or BF16.

You can multiply these tensors with 

F.scaled_mm
, which supports both tensorwise and rowwise scaling. Here's a small example with one scale per tensor:

import torch
import torch.nn.functional as F

def quantize_fp8(x):
    limit = torch.finfo(torch.float8_e4m3fn).max
    scale = x.abs().amax().clamp_min(1e-12) / limit
    return (x / scale).to(torch.float8_e4m3fn), scale

x = torch.randn(1, 1024, device="mps", dtype=torch.float32)
weight = torch.randn(1024, 1024, device="mps", dtype=torch.float32)
x_fp8, x_scale = quantize_fp8(x)
w_fp8, w_scale = quantize_fp8(weight)

y = F.scaled_mm(
    x_fp8,
    w_fp8.t(),
    scale_a=x_scale,
    scale_recipe_a=F.ScalingType.TensorWise,
    scale_b=w_scale,
    scale_recipe_b=F.ScalingType.TensorWise,
    output_dtype=torch.bfloat16,
)
print(y.shape, y.dtype)

Faster language-model decoding

Every LLM has a prefill phase and a decode phase. During decode, each new token goes through the model as a single row, so the big matrix multiplications turn into matrix-vector products. PyTorch 2.15 speeds up both kinds of layers that dominate this step: dense linear layers and mixture-of-experts layers.

Linear layers

MPS has had GEMV kernels for 

torch.mm
since 2.14, but 
F.linear
still went through MPSGraph. PyTorch 2.15 connects them to 
F.linear
, so the common 
[1, 1, hidden_size]
decoding input uses them directly, with eligible bias additions fused in. Across 96 BF16 layer shapes from real models, that's a 1.23× geometric-mean speedup. The biggest wins land on small projections, such as the gates in MoE models, where the old path left most of the memory bandwidth unused. Large layers and LM heads were already close to bandwidth-bound, so they stay near 1×.

Mixture-of-experts layers

A mixture-of-experts layer sends different numbers of tokens to each expert. Grouped matmul handles those uneven groups in a single operation, and 2.15 gives MPS a native implementation.

In 2.14, grouped matmul copied the group offsets to the CPU and looped over the groups. The new Metal kernels read the offsets directly on the GPU, using Metal Performance Primitives where available and a separate Metal path elsewhere. Small groups, the common case during decoding, get their own kernel as well.

For example, 64 tokens can be split into groups of 16, 32, and 16:

import torch
import torch.nn.functional as F

tokens = torch.randn(64, 64, device="mps", dtype=torch.bfloat16)
weights = torch.randn(3, 128, 64, device="mps", dtype=torch.bfloat16)
ends = torch.tensor([16, 48, 64], device="mps", dtype=torch.int32)

out = F.grouped_mm(tokens, weights.transpose(-2, -1), offs=ends)
print(out.shape)  # torch.Size([64, 128])

The decoding kernel shows up directly in token throughput. On an M3 Ultra with 

torch.compile
, MoE models generate about 1.3× more tokens per second:

Linear algebra gets a boost

Complex-valued computations

Working with complex tensors gets easier. 

complex64
LU factorization, LU solve and triangular solve now run on MPS, which also unlocks the operations and gradients built on them, such as complex determinants. Here's a small system solved directly on the GPU:
import torch

a = torch.randn(8, 8, device="mps", dtype=torch.complex64)
a = a + 8 * torch.eye(8, device="mps", dtype=torch.complex64)
b = torch.randn(8, 2, device="mps", dtype=torch.complex64)

lu, pivots = torch.linalg.lu_factor(a)
x = torch.linalg.lu_solve(lu, pivots, b)
print((a @ x - b).abs().max().item())

Small matrices and larger solves

Small matrices get fast kernels too. For camera geometry and image transformations, batches of FP32 matrices up to 4 × 4 are inverted in a single Metal kernel that combines factorization and solving. Larger problems get attention as well: QR uses blocked updates, and triangular solves turn much of their work into efficient matrix multiplication.

Gated DeltaNet workloads get a dedicated fast path for batches of 16 × 16, 32 × 32 and 64 × 64 FP32 triangular systems with at least eight right-hand sides.

SVD is also more robust at numerical extremes. It now correctly handles very small singular values, very large or very small input magnitudes and basis completion with 

full_matrices=True
, which in turn makes pseudoinverse and least-squares results more reliable.

Convolutions, padding, and training

Audio models, video decoders and training loops have their own expensive operations. This release gives several of them new paths through Metal:

OperationWhat changes in 2.15
conv1d
forward		 Specialized kernels replace MPSGraph, plus an im2col-plus-matmul path for short outputs. Useful for audio and streaming-model shapes.
Constant padding Moves to Metal kernels, fixing runaway driver-memory growth in tiled video VAE decoding (more below).
Reflection and replication padding New Metal implementations that are faster and fix backward correctness.
Out-of-place dropout 
nn.Dropout
and 
F.dropout
now use the existing fused kernel.
Upsampling backward A Metal gather kernel replaces the MPSGraph resize-gradient path.
Channels-last 
conv2d
backward		 Stays on an efficient channels-last path instead of an NCHW graph with costly strided access.

Softmax and reductions

Token sampling gets faster in 2.15 as well. 

softmax
and 
log_softmax
 now run on dedicated Metal kernels, and large vocabularies benefit the most: an FP32 softmax over a 

[1, 128256]
row of logits drops from 57 µs to 7 µs, about 8× faster than the MPSGraph version. The speedup holds across other common vocabulary sizes:

A much smaller memory footprint for video decoding

One of the most striking results in this release comes from the constant-padding change. The VAE decode in 

Wan-AI/Wan2.2-TI2V-5B-Diffusers
makes 8,764 padding calls over a full 28-tile decode. With padding on Metal, peak driver memory drops from about 270 GiB to 8 GiB:
Memory metricMPSGraph paddingMetal padding
Current tensor-allocation peak4.422 GiB4.095 GiB
Allocator-reserved peak8.070 GiB8.070 GiB
Total driver-memory peak270.135 GiB8.108 GiB

More control with MPS streams

You can now pick which MPS stream runs your work, directly from Python. 

torch.mps.Stream
and the 
torch.mps.stream
context manager provide the interface, and 
Tensor.record_stream
 lets the allocator track a tensor's use on another stream.

Here's a small example that sends work to a separate stream and synchronizes before reading the result:

import torch

x = torch.randn(1024, device="mps")
torch.mps.synchronize()
worker = torch.mps.Stream()

with torch.mps.stream(worker):
    y = x.square()
    x.record_stream(worker)

del x
worker.synchronize()
print(y.cpu().shape)

More operations work on MPS

Several more operations now run on MPS: 

torch.frexp
, 
torch.logspace
, 
torch.take
and 
Tensor.put_
, 
torch.heaviside
, 
torch.special.laguerre_polynomial_l
 and unsigned-integer comparisons. 

logspace
doesn't yet support integer or boolean outputs with more than one element.

Attention gets a correctness fix too: the MPS math implementation of scaled dot-product attention now handles batch and head broadcasting correctly.

A sneak peek at PyTorch 2.16

Work on 2.16 is already well underway. Some of the changes below have landed on 

main
and are available in the nightlies; others are still in review, so details may change before the release.

Faster LLM decoding

Once a model's decode path no longer contains any MPSGraph ops, the GPU only starts on a token after the CPU has finished encoding all of its kernels. PyTorch 2.16 commits the command buffer every 16 kernels, so the GPU gets to work while the CPU is still encoding the rest. For compiled BF16 decoding at a 2048-token context:

ModelBeforeAfterChange
LFM2.5-8B-A1B108.8 tokens/s126.0 tokens/s+16%
Qwen3.6-35B-A3B52.9 tokens/s62.8 tokens/s+19%
Qwen3.8-27B12.1 tokens/s12.6 tokens/s+4%

Attention runs entirely on Metal

Scaled dot-product attention is dropping MPSGraph completely: every shape will run on Metal kernels, with dedicated vector kernels for decoding and Metal Performance Primitives for half-precision prefill on newer macOS versions. The shapes that used to fall back to MPSGraph benefit the most. On an M5 Pro, decoding with grouped-query attention (32 query heads, 8 KV heads, head dim 80, 4K context) drops from 465 µs to 65 µs, and a 4K × 4K prefill with head dim 40 goes from 42 ms to 6 ms.

More MPSGraph to Metal migrations

The move away from MPSGraph continues. Batch norm forward and backward are in progress, while MSE loss (up to 12× faster on small inputs), 

std_mean
and 
var_mean
 (up to 4× faster) and 
bincount
 have already landed. 

bincount
is the most dramatic: when most values fall into a single bin, counting 4 million integers used to take 6.8 seconds and now takes half a millisecond.

A smaller install

Bundled shaders will build for Metal 3.1 by default, with Metal 4 versions compiled only for the kernels that need them. That shrinks 

libtorch_cpu.dylib
by about 25%, from 384 MiB to 287 MiB, and lays the groundwork for Metal 4.1 shaders with faster matmuls and native FP8 matrix multiplication.

Wrapping up

PyTorch 2.15 brings FP8 to the Mac, faster LLM decoding for dense and MoE models, more linear algebra on the GPU and a long list of operations moved from MPSGraph to dedicated Metal kernels. Give the release candidate a try!

What's next for us

  • More MPS: 2.16 will run attention entirely on Metal, and we'll keep moving operations off MPSGraph.
  • torch.compile
    : we're working on getting rid of graph breaks, so more models compile end to end.
  • Your ideas: what else should we work on in PyTorch? If something is slow, missing or broken, on MPS or anywhere else, open an issue on GitHub and let us know.

A big thank you to Nikita Shulga, Kurt Mohler and Aaron Gokaslan for reviewing much of this work, and to everyone who contributed to MPS in this release.

entries.title: TorchNeuron: running HF models on AWS Trainium is easier than ever
entries.content:
Update on GitHub

TorchNeuron provides a new native backend for PyTorch on AWS Trainium. Transformers, Diffusers and Kernels natively support it, making it easier than ever to run models on Trainium and to share them on the HF hub.

TorchNeuron

TorchNeuron is a PyTorch plugin that brings a new backend for Trainium enabling support for eager mode, 

torch.compile
and native distributed APIs like FSDP and TP. Read the Pytorch blog to learn more about TorchNeuron.

Starting Oct. 20, 2026, TorchNeuron will be available as a public beta. Researchers and developers will be able to install it with 

pip install torch-neuronx
.

New backend, native interface in HF libraries

To date, the Hugging Face experience on AWS Trainium and Inferentia — AI chips designed respectively for cost-effective training and inference at scale — has been delivered through optimum-neuron. This library relies on the torch-neuronx package, which is based on PyTorch XLA. It was the natural choice at the time, but it meant thinking like a compiler: lazy tensors instead of eager execution, static shapes only, a recompilation for every graph break. Optimum Neuron existed to hide that complexity, and maintained custom code (modeling classes, trainers, etc) to do so.

TorchNeuron changes this. It integrates directly into PyTorch and exposes 

neuron
as a native device, with eager execution, PyTorch's own distributed primitives (DTensor, FSDP2) and 
torch.compile
.

For the Hugging Face libraries, Trainium becomes a device like any other: Transformers, Diffusers, Accelerate, PEFT and TRL run on it directly, with the same classes and scripts you would use on any other accelerator. From now on, we recommend that Neuron users use these libraries directly instead of going through Optimum Neuron.

Transformers

Inference

Text generation is now natively supported in Transformers for a wide range of models. With TorchNeuron, 89% of the top 100 most-used text-generation model architectures are supported out of the box, compared to 46% with Optimum Neuron v0.4.5. You just need to pass the 

device_map=neuron
argument in your code and your model will be moved to the Neuron devices.

The following is an example of text-generation with tensor parallelism, which will enable to fully benefit from your Neuron instance. Note that it uses a static cache for generation as this is strongly recommended with Neuron to prevent frequent recompilations.

import os

import torch
import torch.distributed as dist
import torch_neuronx  # noqa: F401
from torch.distributed import DeviceMesh
from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM, AutoTokenizer, GenerationConfig
from transformers.distributed import DistributedConfig
from transformers.generation.configuration_utils import CompileConfig

MODEL_ID = "Qwen/Qwen3.8-27B"
MAX_SEQ_LEN = 1024
PREFILL_CHUNK_SIZE = 512

dist.init_process_group(backend="neuron")
world_size = dist.get_world_size()

model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(
    MODEL_ID,
    dtype=torch.bfloat16,
    distributed_config=DistributedConfig(tp_size=world_size),
    device_mesh=DeviceMesh("neuron", list(range(world_size))),
).eval()

tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(MODEL_ID)
if tokenizer.pad_token is None:
    tokenizer.pad_token = tokenizer.eos_token
tokenizer.padding_side = "left"

inputs = tokenizer.apply_chat_template(
    [{"role": "user", "content": "The future of AI is"}],
    add_generation_prompt=True,
    padding=True,
    tokenizer_kwargs={"pad_to_multiple_of": PREFILL_CHUNK_SIZE},
    return_tensors="pt",
)

generation_config = GenerationConfig(
    max_new_tokens=128,
    do_sample=False,
    use_cache=True,
    pad_token_id=tokenizer.pad_token_id,
    eos_token_id=tokenizer.eos_token_id,
    cache_implementation="static",
    max_cache_len=MAX_SEQ_LEN,
    prefill_chunk_size=PREFILL_CHUNK_SIZE,
    compile_config=CompileConfig(backend="neuron", fullgraph=False, dynamic=False),
)

with torch.no_grad():
    output_ids = model.generate(
        inputs["input_ids"],
        attention_mask=inputs["attention_mask"],
        generation_config=generation_config,
    )

if dist.get_rank() == 0:
    prompt_len = inputs["input_ids"].shape[1]
    print(tokenizer.decode(output_ids[0, prompt_len:], skip_special_tokens=True))

Training

Now that Neuron is a native PyTorch device, training on Trainium uses the same Hugging Face libraries as any other accelerator: Transformers, Accelerate, PEFT and TRL. You no longer need a dedicated trainer or a Neuron-specific fork of the model code. A standard TRL fine-tuning script runs on a Trainium instance with only a few Neuron-specific settings.

Here is a supervised fine-tuning script built on TRL's 

SFTTrainer
. If you have fine-tuned a model with TRL on GPUs before, it should look familiar.
import os

import torch
from datasets import load_dataset
from transformers.distributed import DistributedConfig

from trl import ModelConfig, ScriptArguments, SFTConfig, SFTTrainer, TrlParser


def main(script_args, training_args, model_args):
    # The Neuron backend can't compile Dynamo's automatic dynamic shapes yet (https://github.com/huggingface/trl/issues/7660)
    torch._dynamo.config.automatic_dynamic_shapes = False

    training_args.model_init_kwargs = {
        "revision": model_args.model_revision,
        "trust_remote_code": training_args.trust_remote_code,
        "attn_implementation": model_args.attn_implementation,
        "dtype": model_args.dtype,
        "device_map": None,
    }
    if int(os.environ.get("WORLD_SIZE", "1")) > 1:
        # The model is sharded on the TP x FSDP grid as its weights are loaded
        training_args.model_init_kwargs["distributed_config"] = DistributedConfig(
            tp_size=int(os.environ.get("TP_SIZE", "1")),
            fsdp_size=int(os.environ.get("FSDP_SIZE", "1")),
        )

    # Prepare dataset
    train_dataset = load_dataset(
        script_args.dataset_name,
        name=script_args.dataset_config,
        split=script_args.dataset_train_split,
    )
    # UltraChat also has a string `prompt` column, which makes TRL treat it as a prompt-completion dataset.
    train_dataset = train_dataset.select_columns(["messages"])

    # Training
    trainer = SFTTrainer(
        model=model_args.model_name_or_path,
        args=training_args,
        train_dataset=train_dataset,
    )

    trainer.train()
    trainer.save_model(training_args.output_dir)
    trainer.end()


if __name__ == "__main__":
    parser = TrlParser((ScriptArguments, SFTConfig, ModelConfig))
    script_args, training_args, model_args = parser.parse_args_and_config()
    main(script_args, training_args, model_args)

Parallelism is handled natively by Transformers. You put a 

DistributedConfig
with the tensor-parallel (TP) and FSDP sizes in 
model_init_kwargs
, 
SFTTrainer
passes it to 
from_pretrained
, and the model is sharded as its weights are loaded. The Trainer sees that the model is already distributed and does not wrap it again. You don't need an 
--fsdp
flag or an Accelerate FSDP config.

Nothing in the script is tied to Trainium: the same code runs on any hardware. A few things are worth knowing when you run it on Trainium:

  • Static shapes. The script disables automatic dynamic shapes in 
    torch.compile
    and uses wrapped packing to produce sequences of up to 2048 tokens. With TRL ≥ 1.16, batches on Neuron are padded to a multiple of 128 tokens, limiting the number of input shapes. Compiled graphs are reused for subsequent steps with the same shapes.
  • torch.compile
    on. Passing 
    --torch_compile true
    is all it takes: on a Trainium instance, 
    torch.compile
    detects the device and picks the Neuron backend automatically, with nothing else to configure.
  • Async weight loading off. The built-in asynchronous weight loading in Transformers is not supported on Neuron, so for now we disable it with 
    HF_DEACTIVATE_ASYNC_LOAD=1
    .

The command below launches training with 

torchrun
, which starts one process per NeuronCore. 
TP_SIZE
and 
FSDP_SIZE
set the parallelism layout, and their product is the number of processes: here 4 x 8 = 32, matching 
--nproc_per_node
. The 32 processes form a 4 x 8 grid. Tensor parallelism splits each layer across the 4 cores of a TP group, and FSDP shards the parameters, gradients and optimizer state across the 8 TP groups.
TP_SIZE=4 FSDP_SIZE=8 HF_DEACTIVATE_ASYNC_LOAD=1 uv run torchrun --nproc_per_node=32 sft_neuron_example.py \
    --model_name_or_path Qwen/Qwen3-8B \
    --dataset_name HuggingFaceH4/ultrachat_200k \
    --dataset_train_split train_sft \
    --output_dir Qwen3-8B-sft-tp4-fsdp8 \
    --dtype bfloat16 \
    --max_length 2048 \
    --packing true \
    --packing_strategy wrapped \
    --learning_rate 2e-5 \
    --warmup_steps 0.03 \
    --num_train_epochs 1 \
    --logging_steps 2 \
    --per_device_train_batch_size 4 \
    --gradient_accumulation_steps 4 \
    --save_only_model true \
    --torch_compile true

We ran it on 8 Trainium2 chips (32 NeuronCores), which is half a 

trn2.48xlarge
instance.

Training runs to completion, and 

trainer.save_model
writes a standard Transformers checkpoint. Nothing in it is tied to Neuron: you can push it to the Hugging Face Hub as is and load it on any other hardware.

Diffusers

Inference

Many pipelines from the Diffusers library are compatible with TorchNeuron in eager and compiled mode. FLUX.1-dev, FLUX.2, Qwen-Image, Qwen-Image-2.1 and H3 are also compatible with tensor parallelism to make the most of your Neuron devices. The following is an example showing how you can use TP:

import torch, torch.distributed as dist, torch_neuronx # TP
from torch.distributed.device_mesh import DeviceMesh # TP
from diffusers import QwenImage21Pipeline, QwenImage21Transformer2DModel, TensorParallelConfig

# Distributed devices initialization
dist.init_process_group(backend="neuron") # TP
dev = torch.neuron.current_device()
mesh = DeviceMesh("neuron", list(range(8))) # TP=8

# Pipeline initialization
model = "Qwen/Qwen-Image-2.1"
transformer = QwenImage21Transformer2DModel.from_pretrained(
    model,
    subfolder="transformer",
    torch_dtype=torch.bfloat16,
    parallel_config=TensorParallelConfig(mesh=mesh), # TP
)
pipe = QwenImage21Pipeline.from_pretrained(
    model,
    transformer=transformer,
    torch_dtype=torch.bfloat16,
)
pipe.vae.to(dev)
pipe.transformer.compile_repeated_blocks(backend="neuron", fullgraph=True, dynamic=False)

# Image generation
emb, mask, _ = pipe.encode_prompt(prompt="A capybara wearing a wizard hat, oil painting", device="cpu")  # text encoder stays on CPU
image = pipe(
    prompt_embeds=emb.to(dev),
    prompt_embeds_mask=mask.to(dev) if mask is not None else None,
    height=1024,
    width=1024,
    num_inference_steps=40,
    generator=torch.Generator("cpu").manual_seed(0), # same noise on every rank
).images[0]
if dist.get_rank() == 0:
    image.save("out.png")

You can run this piece of code with: 

NEURON_LOGICAL_NC_CONFIG=2 torchrun --nproc_per_node=8 run.py
.

More and more pipleines will be compatible with TP. If a pipeline you like is not, you can also add support for it following this guide.
